analysis.one_liner: Expands voting access, sets national election standards, and requires disclosure of big political spending.
analysis.headline: The Freedom to Vote Act never received a committee vote or a floor vote in the 118th Congress, despite 217 Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make registering and voting easier nationwide: automatic and same-day registration, online registration, early voting, vote-by-mail, secured drop boxes, and Election Day as a federal holiday. It would set national election-security standards like paper ballots and post-election audits, protect election workers from harassment, ban mid-decade redistricting, and require disclosure of big political spending, including online political ads and anonymous "dark money" donations. It would also create an optional small-dollar public funding system for House campaigns.
analysis.who_benefits: Eligible voters who currently hit barriers: people who move often, work long hours, lack IDs, have disabilities, live far from polling places, or were formerly incarcerated. Election workers gain federal harassment protections. Small donors gain because a matching system amplifies their contributions against big-money campaigns, and all voters gain from disclosure of who funds political ads. States and local election offices gain federal grants to implement the changes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters facing registration and ballot access barriers

how_it_helps.text: Automatically registers eligible voters through state motor vehicle agencies unless they decline, and requires online registration, same-day registration, and Internet-based registration updates.
Requires early voting, vote-by-mail, ballot drop boxes, ballot-tracking, and limits on removing voters from the rolls, and makes Election Day a federal public holiday.
Restores the right to vote in federal elections to citizens who have finished serving a felony sentence, and expands voting access for people with disabilities.
Sets election-security standards: voter-verifiable paper ballots, mandatory post-election audits, U.S.-manufactured voting machines, and grants to states for compliant systems.
Protects election workers and local election administrators: harassment of election workers becomes a federal offense, and administrators get protection from partisan removal.

Requires disclosure of big political money: closes loopholes on foreign-national spending, requires disclaimers and sponsor identification on online political ads, and requires certain tax-exempt organizations to report their large donors.
Creates an optional small-dollar financing program for House candidates with federal matching funds, enhanced support for small donations, and lets candidates use campaign funds for childcare.
Bans mid-decade congressional redistricting and sets criteria for drawing congressional districts, limiting partisan gerrymandering between censuses.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the state implementation grants (the bill authorizes $3 billion for automatic registration in fiscal 2024 plus more in later years) and the small-dollar campaign fund, which is financed by appropriations and by assessments on campaign-finance fines and penalties. States must rework registration, voting, and audit systems to meet federal standards. Large donors, Super PACs, dark-money organizations, and online platforms that run political ads lose the anonymity and freedom from rules they operate under today; platforms also bear compliance costs for ad disclosure.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, large donors, Super PACs, and platforms

drawbacks.text: It is expensive: $3 billion is authorized for fiscal 2024 for automatic registration implementation alone, plus open-ended sums for later years, and a new public campaign-financing program funded by appropriations and assessments on campaign fines.

It overrides state election rules with national mandates covering registration, early voting, mail ballots, audits, and redistricting, which critics view as a federal takeover of elections that states have historically run; the bill itself relies on the constitutional claim that federal election regulation supersedes inconsistent state rules.
It channels all court challenges to the bill's constitutionality into a single court, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, which concentrates review of a sweeping law in one forum.

Its protections for automatic-registration errors bar prosecution or immigration consequences for people registered by mistake, which opponents could argue weakens accountability; the bill still criminalizes knowing, willful false registration and illegal voting.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to voters are broad and durable: a national floor for registration and ballot access, hardened election security, and transparency about who pays for political advertising. The costs are real but modest relative to the stakes: several billion dollars in implementation grants and public campaign funds, and a genuine transfer of election rulemaking from states to the federal government that many will oppose on principle. The single-forum judicial review provision is a design choice that invites criticism. On balance, the bill's main trade is taxpayer money and state autonomy for easier voting, safer elections, and disclosed political money.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in eight committees for the rest of the two-year Congress; no committee ever voted on it and the House never voted on it, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative John Sarbanes introduced the Freedom to Vote Act on July 18, 2023, joined by Representatives Jeffries, Morelle, and Sewell.

The Speaker referred it to eight committees, with House Administration in the lead, and it was later sent to subcommittees on cybersecurity and on Social Security; that is the last action of any kind in the record.
In its roughly seventeen remaining months, the bill received no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote in the House.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large donors, Super PACs, and dark-money spenders are better off because the bill died: the current rules letting them spend without disclosure and without small-dollar competition remain in place, as does the ability of state officials to write election rules without federal standards.

for.name: John Sarbanes
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Freedom to Vote Act and assembled the original cosponsorship.

for.name: Hakeem Jeffries
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor named in the bill's introduction alongside Sarbanes, Morelle, and Sewell.

for.name: 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; no Republican cosponsored the bill.

against.name: House Republican committee chairs
against.role: Chairs of the eight committees of referral, led by the Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or committee vote in any of the eight committees; the action record shows no activity beyond the original referrals and subcommittee assignments.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor at any point in the 118th Congress; no vote ever occurred.

sides.party_line_note: All 217 cosponsors were Democrats and none were Republicans; with the Republican majority controlling the committees and the floor calendar, the bill never advanced past referral.

industries.note: The bill treats coordinated spending as a contribution, requires reporting of large campaign disbursements, and creates a small-dollar matching system that competes with big-check fundraising. Its passage would directly reduce the influence of concentrated campaign money.
The Spotlight Act provision would require certain tax-exempt organizations to list their major contributors on their annual returns, ending anonymous political giving through these groups.

industries.industry: Online platforms and digital political advertisers
industries.note: The Honest Ads provisions would require political ad disclaimers, sponsor-identification notices, and advertiser record-keeping on online platforms, and would extend the foreign-money ban to online political advertising.

Mandatory voter-verifiable paper ballots and U.S.-manufactured machines would force replacement purchases, and the bill authorizes federal grants to states for compliant paper-ballot systems and security upgrades.

States keep their role as the operators of elections but gain federal money and permanent federal standards for registration, voting access, audits, and list maintenance; their systems become the funded channel for the new national rules.
